chapter_theme: The lovers turn the town's gossip around. Talk meant to shame and stop them feeds the love, keeps the man alive, and can even press for marriage or elopement. The chapter treats public scandal as an unintended gift.
structure_note: On Parimelazhagar's headnotes, the man speaks 1141-1145 and the woman 1146-1149, usually with the man overhearing, and 1150 is the friend's. He says the twenty verses of chapters 114 and 115 belong to the preliminary conditions of union (புணர்தல் நிமித்தம்).

1141.reading: A precious life holds on because the gossip has risen, and by good fortune the many don't know this; for Parimelazhagar the man speaks of his own life, while Manakkudavar speaks of her life and leaves the speaker unnamed.
1141.nuance: The joke rests on the second line: if the gossips knew they were helping, they would stop. Commentators differ on the source of luck. Parimelazhagar says தெய்வத்தால் and Manakkudavar says புண்ணியத்தாலே; one is divine and the other is merit, for a verse whose word is the Sanskrit-derived பாக்கியம்.

positions.position: The man, unable to reach her, is sustained by talk that makes her seem attainable.
positions.quote: அங்ஙனம் அரியாளை எளியளாக்கி எடுக்கின்றமையின், அஃது அவ்வாருயிர்க்குப் பற்றுக்கோடாக நின்றது

positions.position: It is her life that the gossip sustains.
It is the couple's life, which survives on hope that talk will help their love succeed.

1142.reading: The man says this town, not knowing how rare the flower-eyed woman is, has made him a present of gossip.
1142.nuance: ஈந்தது is the verb for a generous gift. Parimelazhagar takes it that way, as an ironic thanks. The rarity differs by commentator: for Parimelazhagar, she is hard to reach, and for Manakkudavar, it is her noble birth that the gossips ignore.

1143.reading: The man asks whether the gossip the whole town knows isn't his to have, since it feels like having what he hasn't yet obtained.
1143.nuance: The gossip isn't true yet, and that is its use: being talked about as a couple gives a foretaste of being one. Manakkudavar gives a more practical reason, in which the man tells the friend that the talk will bring the families round.

1144.reading: The man says gossip makes his love flourish, and that without it the love would lose its nature and droop.
1144.nuance: The sound carries the argument: கவ்வை, கவ்விது, தவ்வென்னும். Parimelazhagar explains கவ்விது as a coinage from the noun, and தவ் as a word that imitates sagging. The claim is that love depends in part on being seen.

1145.reading: Love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking becomes more desired each time one gets drunk; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The man says that his own desire is so strong that gossip itself gives him pleasure.
positions.quote: வேட்கை மிகுதியால் அலரும் இன்பஞ் செய்யாநின்றது என்பதாம்.

positions.position: The friend replies to the man, who has asked whether this gossip is hurting them.
positions.quote: நுமக்குத் துன்பமாயிற்றே இவ்வலரென்று வினாவிய தலைமகற்குத் தோழி கூறியது.

1146.reading: The woman says she saw him on only one day, and the gossip has spread like the serpent seizing the moon.
1146.nuance: An eclipse is an event no one can miss, and a tiny private act is set against it. Parimelazhagar has her speaking to her friend with the man in earshot, so the complaint is really a demand for marriage. Kalaignar pauses to mark the serpent as an imaginary notion, which the commentators before him don't do.

1147.reading: The woman says this sickness grows long, with the town's gossip as its manure and her mother's words as its water.
1147.nuance: Whatever is meant to shrink the love feeds it, as Parimelazhagar spells out. The one verse in the chapter to name her mother shows where the gossip actually hurts: at home. Parimelazhagar takes ஊரவர் to mean the women of the town.

1148.reading: The woman says that to think gossip can put out love is like thinking ghee can put out fire.
1148.nuance: The grammar frames this as an error in thought, 'to say we will extinguish'. Parimelazhagar places it in the same scene as 1147, so it is also her answer to the friend's advice that she should take the talk seriously and bear up.

1149.reading: The woman asks how she can be ashamed of gossip when the man who told her not to fear has left her, in a way that shames everyone who sees it.
1149.nuance: This verse is the turn in the chapter, with gossip now no longer a game. The promise 'fear not' is quoted against him. Shame has moved from what she feels about the town to what those watching feel on her behalf, so she has none left to spend on rumour.

1150.reading: The speaker, whom Parimelazhagar identifies as the friend talking to the woman while the man overhears, says the town is raising the very gossip they want, and the lover will grant it if asked or if he wishes.

positions.position: தாம் வேண்டின் means 'if we ask', and the friend is steering the man towards elopement, which the gossip now justifies.
positions.quote: இனிக் காதலர்தாமும்யாம் வேண்டியக்கால் அதனை இனிதின் நேர்வர்

positions.position: The words mean 'if the lover also wishes', and his consent depends on his own desire.

links.note: 183 says that it is better to die than to live by backbiting, because it is a false kind of life. In 1141 backbiting is what keeps someone else alive. The same act has a very different moral look from the side of its target.

930 asks whether a sober drunkard, seeing another drunk, doesn't recognise his own degradation. 1145 takes the same compulsion, wanting more with each intoxication, and uses it with delight. The book that condemns drink reuses its logic to describe love without condemning it.
In 1093, the water poured into love's plot is her lowered glance. In 1147 the water is her mother's harsh words. What nourishes love moves from the most private gesture to the most hostile.

source_issues: 1141: Parimelazhagar's headnote has வந்த தலைமகளை ... அவள் சொல்லியது, but his gloss clearly has a male speaker who can't reach her and says கூறினான். The feminine forms look like errors for தலைமகனை and அவன்.

1141: Manakkudavar's entry ends with களவியல் முற்றிற்று, so his sequence ends the secret-love section at this verse, and his order seems to differ from the one used here. That may also explain why he has no aligned entry for 1144, 1147, 1148 and 1150.
